questions.canonical: Is the moral status of an act grounded in revelation or in reason?
questions.plain: Do things become right because God says so, or can we work out right and wrong ourselves?
questions.technicalName: husn wa qubh / divine command vs. moral rationalism

positions.label: Divine Command Theory (revelation-grounded)
positions.definition: An act's moral status is constituted by God's command; acts have no intrinsic value prior to the decree.

positions.label: Moral rationalism / ethical objectivism (reason-grounded)
positions.definition: Acts have intrinsic husn/qubh knowable by reason (aql) independently of revelation.

holds.scholarlyDispute: Osborne (Religious Studies 41:1, 2005, DOI 10.1017/S0034412504007218) reads Ockham as divine-command theorist; others deny.

holds.qualification: rationalism via autonomy of practical reason, not value-realism

equivalences.evidence: Both ground value in divine will (al-Islam.org on Ashari 'a'rad'; Osborne on Ockham 'God could assign a different moral value'); but Ashari occasionalism/kasb has no Ockhamist parallel.
Both hold reason knows objective value, but Abd al-Jabbar is a value-realist (Hourani 1971) while Kant is a constructivist.

passages.text: Goodness and badness of actions (husn wa qubh) are not qualities inhering in them; these are mere accidents (a'rad).
passages.citation: M. Abdul Hye, 'Ash'arism', A History of Muslim Philosophy vol.1, via al-islam.org

passages.text: human reason can independently judge the good or evil in things ... independently of the commands of the Shari'ah.
passages.citation: Mutahhari, An Introduction to Ilm al-Kalam, via al-islam.org
